notes.front: What is the GitHub Advisory Database?
notes.back: GitHub’s curated list of security vulnerabilities, which you can view, search and filter.
notes.explanation: You use it to understand and remediate the risks in your dependencies.
notes.example: Like a public register of product recalls: you look up the parts you use to see whether any have been recalled.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub security features”, “GitHub Advisory Database”
notes.evidence: The GitHub Advisory Database contains a curated list of security vulnerabilities that you can view, search, and filter.

notes.front: What is the Open Source Vulnerability format (OSV)?
notes.back: The `JSON` format in which advisories in the GitHub Advisory Database are published.
notes.explanation: Every advisory in the database is published in this format.
notes.example: Like a standard shipping label: any courier can read it, whichever depot printed it.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advisory database”, “About the GitHub Advisory Database”
notes.evidence: Security advisories are published as JSON files in the Open Source Vulnerability (OSV) format.

notes.front: What is Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE)?
notes.back: A list of publicly known vulnerabilities, each with a CVE identification number; GitHub’s advisory form matches its description format.
notes.explanation: GitHub’s security advisories build on the CVE list.
notes.example: Like a catalogue number for a known fault, so everyone discussing it means the same one.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Repository security advisories”, “CVE identification numbers”
notes.evidence: GitHub Security Advisories builds upon the foundation of the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) list. The security advisory form on GitHub is a standardized form that matches the CVE description format.

notes.front: What is a CVE Numbering Authority (CNA)?
notes.back: An organisation authorised to assign CVE identification numbers. GitHub is one.
notes.explanation: Because GitHub is a CNA, it can give your project a CVE identification number.
notes.example: Like a registry office allowed to issue certificates: only offices so authorised can issue the numbers.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Repository security advisories”, “CVE identification numbers”
notes.evidence: GitHub is a CVE Numbering Authority (CNA) and is authorized to assign CVE identification numbers.

notes.front: What is Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE)?
notes.back: A catalogue of weakness types, each with an identifier such as CWE-400, Uncontrolled Resource Consumption; CVEs are tagged with them.
notes.explanation: GitHub uses CWE tags, for example to filter low-impact alerts in a preset rule.
notes.example: A CVE is one particular broken lock; its CWE is the kind of flaw, like “latch can be slipped”.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “CWEs used by GitHub’s preset Dependabot rules”, “Dismiss low impact issues for development-scoped dependencies”
notes.evidence: we use the following GitHub-curated Common Weakness Enumerations (CWEs) to filter out low impact alerts

notes.front: What is the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS)?
notes.back: The scoring system whose four severity levels (Low, Medium/Moderate, High, Critical) the GitHub Advisory Database uses.
notes.explanation: It rates how severe a vulnerability is, which is different from how likely it is to be exploited.
notes.example: Like a storm warning’s colour: it says how bad the damage could be, not whether the storm will hit you.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advisory database”, “CVSS levels”
notes.evidence: The severity level is one of four possible levels defined in the [Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS), Section 5](https://www.first.org/cvss/specification-document).

notes.front: What is the Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS)?
notes.back: A system from the Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams that estimates the likelihood a vulnerability will be exploited.
notes.explanation: Its score is a probability between 0 and 1: the higher it is, the likelier exploitation.
notes.example: Like a weather forecast’s chance of rain: 0.8 means rain is likely, whatever size the storm.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advisory database”, “EPSS scores”
notes.evidence: The Exploit Prediction Scoring System, or EPSS, is a system devised by the global Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams (FIRST) for quantifying the likelihood of vulnerability exploit.

notes.front: What is the EPSS percentile?
notes.back: The proportion of all scored vulnerabilities with the same or a lower EPSS score.
notes.explanation: It ranks a vulnerability against the others, rather than giving its own probability.
notes.example: Like a runner’s place in a race: the 90th percentile beats 90% of the field, whatever the time.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advisory database”, “EPSS scores”
notes.evidence: GitHub also displays the EPSS score percentile, which is the proportion of all scored vulnerabilities with the same or a lower EPSS score.

notes.front: What is a GitHub-reviewed advisory?
notes.back: An advisory that GitHub has reviewed for validity and mapped to a package in a supported ecosystem, with a full description.
notes.explanation: It is the kind of advisory that notifies you about packages you depend on.
notes.example: Like a recall notice checked by an inspector and tied to an exact model number.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advisory database”, “GitHub-reviewed vulnerability advisories”
notes.evidence: GitHub-reviewed** advisories are mapped to packages in ecosystems we support. We carefully review each advisory for validity and ensure that they contain a full description and both ecosystem and package information.

notes.front: What is an unreviewed advisory?
notes.back: An advisory published automatically into the GitHub Advisory Database straight from the National Vulnerability Database feed.
notes.explanation: It has not been checked for validity or completion.
notes.example: Like a news wire item printed as received, before an editor has checked it.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advisory database”, “Unreviewed vulnerability advisories”
notes.evidence: Unreviewed** advisories are published automatically into the GitHub Advisory Database, directly from the National Vulnerability Database feed.

notes.front: What is a malware advisory?
notes.back: An advisory about a malicious open source package.
notes.explanation: Malware is intentionally designed to do harm, unlike an accidental vulnerability.
notes.example: A warning that a package on a public registry was published by an attacker, not by the team you think.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advisory database”, “Malware advisories”
notes.evidence: Malware** advisories are advisories about malicious open source packages.

notes.front: What is a GHSA ID?
notes.back: The unique identifier every advisory in the GitHub Advisory Database has, whatever its type.
notes.explanation: It is assigned when an advisory is created on GitHub or added from a supported source.
notes.example: Like a case number that every report gets, whether or not it also has a CVE number.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advisory database”, “GHSA IDs”
notes.evidence: Each security advisory, regardless of its type, has a unique identifier referred to as a GHSA ID.

notes.front: What is a repository security advisory?
notes.back: An advisory that lets maintainers of a public repository privately discuss and fix a vulnerability, then publish it to their community.
notes.explanation: Publishing makes it easier for users to update dependencies and research the impact.
notes.example: A maintainer hears of a flaw in her date library, fixes it out of sight, then announces it with the patched version.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Repository security advisories”, “About repository security advisories”
notes.evidence: Repository security advisories allow maintainers of public repositories to privately discuss and fix a security vulnerability in a project.

notes.front: What does each advisory in the GitHub Advisory Database relate to?
notes.back: A specific security problem in a software component.
notes.explanation: These problems come in several varieties, such as vulnerabilities and malware.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advisory database”, “Types of security advisories”
notes.evidence: Each advisory in the GitHub Advisory Database relates to a specific security problem in a software component.

notes.front: A vulnerability is a problem in a project’s code that could be exploited to damage the {{c1::confidentiality, integrity, or availability}} of the project or of projects that use it.
notes.explanation: This is the definition the Docs use for vulnerability advisories.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advisory database”, “Types of security advisories”
notes.evidence: A vulnerability is a problem in a project's code that could be exploited to damage the confidentiality, integrity, or availability of the project or other projects that use it.

notes.front: How are vulnerabilities in code usually introduced, and when are they usually fixed?
notes.back: Usually by accident, and usually fixed soon after they are discovered.
notes.explanation: The Docs contrast this with malware, which is intentional.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advisory database”, “Types of security advisories”
notes.evidence: Vulnerabilities in code are usually introduced by accident and fixed soon after they are discovered.

notes.front: Which two pieces of version information does a vulnerability advisory contain?
notes.back: The range of released package versions where the problem exists, and the earliest version where it was fixed.
notes.explanation: This helps downstream users update their dependencies to a fixed version.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advisory database”, “Types of security advisories”
notes.evidence: Vulnerability advisories contain information about the range of released package versions where the problem exists, and the earliest version where the problem was fixed.

notes.front: How do the Docs define malware?
notes.back: Code intentionally designed to perform unwanted or harmful functions.
notes.explanation: It may target hardware, software, confidential data, or users of any application that uses it.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advisory database”, “Types of security advisories”
notes.evidence: In contrast, malicious software, or malware, is code that is intentionally designed to perform unwanted or harmful functions.

notes.front: Why do malware alerts not contain a fix version?
notes.back: Because there are no safe versions: the only safe course is not to use the package at all.
notes.explanation: You remove the malware and find a more secure replacement for the dependency.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advisory database”, “Types of security advisories”
notes.evidence: Malware alerts do not contain a fix version, because the defining characteristic of a malware alert is that there are no safe versions—the only safe course of action is not to use the package at all.

notes.front: Vulnerability advisory versus malware advisory: what does each tell you to do?
notes.back: A vulnerability: update to a fixed version. Malware: remove the package and find a more secure replacement.
notes.explanation: Vulnerabilities are usually accidental and fixable; malware has no safe version.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advisory database”, “Types of security advisories”
notes.evidence: You need to remove the malware from your project and find an alternative, more secure replacement for the dependency.

notes.front: What are two ecosystem advisory databases that the GitHub Advisory Database imports from?
notes.back: Any two of: npm Security advisories, FriendsOfPHP, Go Vulncheck, Python Packaging Advisory, Ruby Advisory, RustSec Advisory.
notes.explanation: The Docs list these alongside GitHub-reported advisories and the National Vulnerability Database.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advisory database”, “GitHub-reviewed vulnerability advisories”
notes.evidence: The [Go Vulncheck database](https://pkg.go.dev/vuln/) * The [Python Packaging Advisory database](https://github.com/pypa/advisory-database) * The [Ruby Advisory database](https://rubysec.com/) * The [RustSec Advisory database](https://rustsec.org/)

notes.front: How does GitHub generally name its supported ecosystems?
notes.back: After the programming language’s associated package registry.
notes.explanation: GitHub reviews advisories for vulnerabilities in packages from a supported registry.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advisory database”, “GitHub-reviewed vulnerability advisories”
notes.evidence: Generally, we name our supported ecosystems after the software programming language's associated package registry.

notes.front: Is GitHub Actions a supported ecosystem for GitHub-reviewed advisories?
notes.back: Yes. Its packages come from GitHub Marketplace.
notes.explanation: The list mixes language registries with GitHub’s own Actions ecosystem.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advisory database”, “GitHub-reviewed vulnerability advisories”
notes.evidence: GitHub Actions (<https://github.com/marketplace?type=actions>) * Maven (registry: <https://repo.maven.apache.org/maven2>)

notes.front: What are two supported ecosystems, with their registries?
notes.back: Any two, for example: Npm (npmjs.com); Pip (pypi.org); Maven; NuGet; RubyGems; Rust (crates.io).
notes.explanation: The list also includes Composer, Erlang, Go, Pub, GitHub Actions and Swift.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advisory database”, “GitHub-reviewed vulnerability advisories”
notes.evidence: * Npm (registry: <https://www.npmjs.com/>) * NuGet (registry: <https://www.nuget.org/>) * Pip (registry: <https://pypi.org/>)

notes.front: If Dependabot alerts are on for your repositories, which advisories notify you about a package you depend on?
notes.back: New GitHub-reviewed advisories that report a vulnerability in that package.
notes.explanation: Only reviewed advisories are mapped to packages in supported ecosystems.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advisory database”, “GitHub-reviewed vulnerability advisories”
notes.evidence: If you enable Dependabot alerts for your repositories, you are automatically notified when a new GitHub-reviewed advisory reports a vulnerability for a package you depend on.

notes.front: Why does Dependabot not create alerts for unreviewed advisories?
notes.back: Because this type of advisory is not checked for validity or completion.
notes.explanation: Unreviewed advisories come straight from the National Vulnerability Database feed.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advisory database”, “Unreviewed vulnerability advisories”
notes.evidence: Dependabot doesn't create Dependabot alerts for unreviewed advisories as this type of advisory isn't checked for validity or completion.

notes.front: GitHub-reviewed versus unreviewed advisory: how does each reach the database, and which raises Dependabot alerts?
notes.back: Reviewed: checked by GitHub and mapped to a package, and it alerts. Unreviewed: imported automatically from the National Vulnerability Database, and it does not.
notes.explanation: The review for validity and completeness is what makes an advisory usable for alerts.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advisory database”, “Unreviewed vulnerability advisories”
notes.evidence: Unreviewed** advisories are published automatically into the GitHub Advisory Database, directly from the National Vulnerability Database feed.

notes.front: From which two sources does GitHub publish malware advisories automatically?
notes.back: The npm security team, and the OpenSSF Malicious Packages repository.
notes.explanation: Malware advisories are about malicious open source packages.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advisory database”, “Malware advisories”
notes.evidence: We publish them automatically into the GitHub Advisory Database from the npm security team and the [OpenSSF Malicious Packages](https://github.com/ossf/malicious-packages) repository.

notes.front: Which search finds malware advisories in the GitHub Advisory Database?
notes.back: `type:malware`.
notes.explanation: Malware advisories sit in the same database as vulnerability advisories.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advisory database”, “Malware advisories”
notes.evidence: You can view malware advisories by searching for `type:malware` in the GitHub Advisory Database.

notes.front: What kind of attack are most malware advisories about?
notes.back: Substitution attacks: publishing a package with the same name as a dependency users get from a third party or private registry.
notes.explanation: The attacker hopes the malicious public version is consumed instead.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advisory database”, “Malware advisories”
notes.evidence: Our malware advisories are mostly about substitution attacks. During this type of attack, an attacker publishes a package to the public registry with the same name as a dependency that users rely on from a third party or private registry

notes.front: Why may a malware alert fire even if you use the safe private package of the same name?
notes.back: Dependabot does not look at project configurations to see whether a package comes from a private registry.
notes.explanation: The Docs add that appropriately scoped dependencies should not be affected by malware.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advisory database”, “Malware advisories”
notes.evidence: Dependabot doesn't look at project configurations to determine if the packages are coming from a private registry, so we can't determine whether you're using the malicious version or a non-malicious version that has the same name.

notes.front: When is a GHSA ID assigned?
notes.back: When a new advisory is created on GitHub, or added to the GitHub Advisory Database from any supported source.
notes.explanation: Every advisory gets one, whatever its type.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advisory database”, “GHSA IDs”
notes.evidence: A `GHSA-ID` qualifier is assigned when a new advisory is created on GitHub or added to the GitHub Advisory Database from any of the supported sources.

notes.front: What is the format of a GHSA ID?
notes.back: `GHSA-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx`, where each x is a lowercase letter or digit from `23456789cfghjmpqrvwx`, randomly assigned.
notes.explanation: The fixed prefix is followed by three groups of four characters.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advisory database”, “GHSA IDs”
notes.evidence: The syntax of GHSA IDs follows this format: `GHSA-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx` where: * `x` is a letter or a number from the following set: `23456789cfghjmpqrvwx`.

notes.front: Which two CVSS versions does the GitHub Advisory Database support?
notes.back: CVSS version 3.1 and CVSS version 4.0.
notes.explanation: Imported CVEs can also carry version 3.0.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advisory database”, “CVSS levels”
notes.evidence: The GitHub Advisory Database supports both CVSS version 3.1 and CVSS version 4.0.

notes.front: Which CVSS versions apply when GitHub obtains a CVE, and when the CVE is imported?
notes.back: Obtained: the version the maintainer assigned, 3.1 or 4.0. Imported: 4.0, 3.1 or 3.0.
notes.explanation: Only imported CVEs can carry the older 3.0 version.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advisory database”, “CVSS levels”
notes.evidence: If GitHub obtains a CVE, the GitHub Advisory Database uses the CVSS version assigned by the maintainer, which can be version 3.1 or 4.0. If the CVE is imported, the GitHub Advisory Database supports CVSS versions 4.0, 3.1 and 3.0.

notes.front: What is the lowest of the four CVSS severity levels the database uses?
notes.back: Low.
notes.explanation: The four levels run Low, Medium/Moderate, High, Critical.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advisory database”, “CVSS levels”
notes.evidence: Low * Medium/Moderate * High * Critical The GitHub Advisory Database uses the CVSS levels described above.

notes.front: In the database’s CVSS levels, which name is paired with “Medium”?
notes.back: “Moderate”: the level is written Medium/Moderate.
notes.explanation: It is the second of the four levels.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advisory database”, “CVSS levels”
notes.evidence: Low * Medium/Moderate * High * Critical

notes.front: What is the highest of the four CVSS severity levels?
notes.back: Critical.
notes.explanation: It sits above High.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advisory database”, “CVSS levels”
notes.evidence: Medium/Moderate * High * Critical The GitHub Advisory Database uses the CVSS levels

notes.front: What are three kinds of information a security advisory may include?
notes.back: Any three of: description, severity, affected package, ecosystem, affected and patched versions, impact.
notes.explanation: References, workarounds and credits are optional extras.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advisory database”, “CVSS levels”
notes.evidence: Each security advisory contains information about the vulnerability or malware, which may include the description, severity, affected package, package ecosystem, affected versions and patched versions, impact, and optional information such as references, workarounds, and credits.

notes.front: What range does an EPSS score take, and what does a higher score mean?
notes.back: Between 0 and 1 (0 and 100%); the higher the score, the greater the probability of exploitation.
notes.explanation: It is a probability, not a severity rating.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advisory database”, “EPSS scores”
notes.evidence: The model produces a probability score between 0 and 1 (0 and 100%), where the higher the score, the greater the probability that a vulnerability will be exploited.

notes.front: Which advisories in the GitHub Advisory Database carry EPSS scores?
notes.back: Advisories containing CVEs that have corresponding EPSS data.
notes.explanation: The scores come from the Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams, not from GitHub.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advisory database”, “EPSS scores”
notes.evidence: The GitHub Advisory Database includes EPSS scores from FIRST for advisories containing CVEs with corresponding EPSS data.

notes.front: An advisory’s EPSS score is 0.42. What does that mean, per the EPSS model?
notes.back: A 42% chance of the vulnerability being exploited in the wild in the next 30 days.
notes.explanation: The Docs’ worked interpretation is expressed over the next 30 days.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advisory database”, “EPSS scores”
notes.evidence: There is a 90.534% chance of this vulnerability being exploited in the wild in the next 30 days.

notes.front: An advisory sits at the 80th EPSS percentile. What does that mean?
notes.back: 80% of all modelled vulnerabilities are considered less likely to be exploited in the next 30 days.
notes.explanation: The percentile compares the vulnerability with all the others scored.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advisory database”, “EPSS scores”
notes.evidence: 95% of the total modeled vulnerabilities are considered less likely to be exploited in the next 30 days than this vulnerability.

notes.front: How does GitHub keep EPSS data up to date?
notes.back: With a daily synchronisation: score percentages are always fully synchronised, percentiles only when significantly different.
notes.explanation: Percentages and percentiles are therefore updated on different terms.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advisory database”, “EPSS scores”
notes.evidence: GitHub keeps EPSS data up to date with a daily synchronization action. While EPSS score percentages will always be fully synchronized, score percentiles will only be updated when significantly different.

notes.front: Can a community contribution edit an advisory’s EPSS data?
notes.back: No. GitHub does not author EPSS data but sources it from the Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams.
notes.explanation: Data GitHub does not author is not editable through community contributions.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advisory database”, “EPSS scores”
notes.evidence: At GitHub, we do not author this data, but rather source it from FIRST, which means that this data is not editable in community contributions.

notes.front: CVSS versus EPSS: what does each measure?
notes.back: CVSS gives a vulnerability’s severity level; EPSS gives the probability it will be exploited.
notes.explanation: A severe vulnerability can still be unlikely to be exploited, and the reverse.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advisory database”, “EPSS scores”
notes.evidence: The Exploit Prediction Scoring System, or EPSS, is a system devised by the global Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams (FIRST) for quantifying the likelihood of vulnerability exploit.

notes.front: EPSS score versus EPSS percentile: what does each tell you?
notes.back: The score is the probability of exploitation in the next 30 days; the percentile ranks that score against all other scored vulnerabilities.
notes.explanation: The Docs say both can be used to interpret the likelihood of exploitation.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advisory database”, “EPSS scores”
notes.evidence: This information helps you understand how both percentage and percentile can be used to interpret the likelihood that a vulnerability could be exploited in the wild

notes.front: What is a community contribution to the GitHub Advisory Database?
notes.back: A pull request to the `github/advisory-database` repository that improves a global security advisory.
notes.explanation: The GitHub Security Lab curation team reviews it and publishes it if accepted.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advisory database”, “Community contributions”
notes.evidence: A **community contribution** is a pull request submitted to the [github/advisory-database](https://github.com/github/advisory-database?ref_product=security-advisories\&ref_type=engagement\&ref_style=text) repository that improves the content of a global security advisory.

notes.front: When GitHub adds a security query to its default or extended suite, how does it calculate the query’s security severity?
notes.back: It takes the 75th percentile of the CVSS scores of all CVEs tagged with the query’s CWE tags.
notes.explanation: Alerts then show that score translated to Critical, High, Medium or Low.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Code scanning alerts”, “Calculation of security severity levels”
notes.evidence: Search for all CVEs that are assigned one or more of the CWE tags associated with the new security query. 2. Calculate the 75th percentile of the CVSS score for those CVEs.

notes.front: Which weakness does CWE-400 name?
notes.back: Uncontrolled Resource Consumption.
notes.explanation: It is one of the GitHub-curated weaknesses used by a preset rule to filter low-impact alerts.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “CWEs used by GitHub’s preset Dependabot rules”, “Dismiss low impact issues for development-scoped dependencies”
notes.evidence: CWE-400 Uncontrolled Resource Consumption

notes.front: CVE versus CWE: what does each identify?
notes.back: A CVE identifies one specific vulnerability; a CWE names a type of weakness, which CVEs can be tagged with.
notes.explanation: GitHub finds CVEs by the CWE tags assigned to them.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Code scanning alerts”, “Calculation of security severity levels”
notes.evidence: Search for all CVEs that are assigned one or more of the CWE tags

notes.front: With repository security advisories, what is the first step for a newly reported vulnerability?
notes.back: Create a draft security advisory and use it to discuss the impact privately.
notes.explanation: Discussion stays private until the maintainers choose to publish.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Repository security advisories”, “About repository security advisories”
notes.evidence: Create a draft security advisory, and use the draft to privately discuss the impact of the vulnerability on your project.

notes.front: Where do maintainers collaborate on the fix for a repository security advisory?
notes.back: In a temporary private fork.
notes.explanation: The fix is worked on out of public view.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Repository security advisories”, “About repository security advisories”
notes.evidence: Privately collaborate to fix the vulnerability in a temporary private fork.

notes.front: When do the Docs say to publish a repository security advisory?
notes.back: Once a patch is released, to alert your community.
notes.explanation: Publishing makes it easier for users to update dependencies.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Repository security advisories”, “About repository security advisories”
notes.evidence: Publish the security advisory to alert your community of the vulnerability once a patch is released.

notes.front: What can a project add to tell people how to report security vulnerabilities to it?
notes.back: A security policy with instructions for reporting vulnerabilities in the project.
notes.explanation: The policy holds instructions for reporting vulnerabilities in your project.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Repository security advisories”, “About repository security advisories”
notes.evidence: You can create a security policy to give people instructions for reporting security vulnerabilities in your project.

notes.front: Which repository security advisories does GitHub publish to the GitHub Advisory Database?
notes.back: Those for any ecosystem supported by the dependency graph; the advisory also stays in your repository.
notes.explanation: npm advisories are also published to the npm security advisories.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Repository security advisories”, “About repository security advisories”
notes.evidence: If you created a security advisory in your repository, the security advisory will stay in your repository. We publish security advisories for any of the ecosystems supported by the dependency graph to the GitHub Advisory Database

notes.front: After a draft advisory from a public repository is published, who sees what?
notes.back: Anyone sees the current advisory data and accepted credits; collaborators can also view the conversation history.
notes.explanation: The advisory’s web address does not change after publication.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Repository security advisories”, “Publication of security advisories”
notes.evidence: Anyone** can see the current version of the advisory data, as well as any advisory credits that the credited users have accepted. * **Collaborators** can view the conversation history of the advisory.

notes.front: When you create a security advisory for a public repository, what are your two options for a CVE identification number?
notes.back: Provide an existing one, or request one from GitHub.
notes.explanation: GitHub can assign numbers because it is a CNA.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Repository security advisories”, “CVE identification numbers”
notes.evidence: you have the option of providing an existing CVE identification number for the security vulnerability. If you want a CVE identification number for the security vulnerability in your project, and don't already have one, you can request a CVE identification number from GitHub.

notes.front: GitHub usually reviews a request for a CVE identification number within {{c1::72 hours}}.
notes.explanation: The Docs say “usually”, so it is not a guarantee.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Repository security advisories”, “CVE identification numbers”
notes.evidence: GitHub usually reviews the request within 72 hours.

notes.front: Does requesting a CVE identification number make your security advisory public?
notes.back: No. GitHub reserves the number and publishes the CVE details only after you make the advisory public.
notes.explanation: You can request the number while the advisory is still a draft.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Repository security advisories”, “CVE identification numbers”
notes.evidence: Requesting a CVE identification number doesn't make your security advisory public. If your security advisory is eligible for a CVE, GitHub will reserve a CVE identification number for your advisory. We'll then publish the CVE details after you make your security advisory public.

notes.front: Who can request a CVE identification number for a security advisory?
notes.back: Anyone with admin permissions to the security advisory.
notes.explanation: The Docs grant this to people with admin permissions on the advisory itself.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Repository security advisories”, “CVE identification numbers”
notes.evidence: Anyone with admin permissions to a security advisory can request a CVE identification number.

notes.front: Your project is covered by a CNA other than GitHub. Can GitHub assign it a CVE?
notes.back: No. Add the CVE from your own CNA to the security advisory form instead.
notes.explanation: GitHub cannot assign CVEs to a project covered by another CNA.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Repository security advisories”, “CVE identification numbers”
notes.evidence: GitHub cannot assign CVEs to your project if it is covered by another CNA.

notes.front: After you publish a repository security advisory, what does GitHub do with it?
notes.back: Reviews it, adds it to the GitHub Advisory Database, and may use it to send Dependabot alerts to affected repositories.
notes.explanation: This can take up to 72 hours, and GitHub may ask you for more information.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Repository security advisories”, “Dependabot alerts for published security advisories”
notes.evidence: GitHub will review each published security advisory, add it to the GitHub Advisory Database, and may use the security advisory to send Dependabot alerts to affected repositories.

notes.front: What should you add to a security advisory before publishing it, whenever possible?
notes.back: A fix version.
notes.explanation: Without one, users are alerted with no safe version to update to.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Repository security advisories”, “Importance of fix versions”
notes.evidence: Whenever possible, you should **add a fix version to a security advisory prior to publishing the advisory**. If you don't, the advisory will be published without a fixed version, and Dependabot will alert your users about the issue, without offering any safe version to update to.

notes.front: The fix version is imminently available. What do the Docs advise, if you are able to?
notes.back: Wait to disclose the issue until the fix is ready.
notes.explanation: Then the advisory can be published with a safe version.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Repository security advisories”, “Importance of fix versions”
notes.evidence: Imminently available**, and you are able to, wait to disclose the issue when the fix is ready.

notes.front: The fix is in development but not yet available. What do the Docs advise?
notes.back: Say so in the advisory, and edit the advisory after publication.
notes.explanation: Published advisories can be edited later.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Repository security advisories”, “Importance of fix versions”
notes.evidence: In development but not yet available**, mention this in the advisory, and edit the advisory later, after publication.

notes.front: No fix is planned. What do the Docs advise putting in the advisory?
notes.back: Say clearly that no fix is planned, and helpfully include steps users can take to mitigate the issue.
notes.explanation: Being clear stops users contacting you to ask when a fix will come.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Repository security advisories”, “Importance of fix versions”
notes.evidence: Not planned**, be clear about it in the advisory so that your users don't contact you to ask when a fix will be made. In this case, it is helpful to include steps users can take to mitigate the issue.

notes.front: A new vulnerability appears in the GitHub Advisory Database as an unreviewed advisory for a package your repository uses. Dependabot alerts are on. What happens?
notes.back: C: No Dependabot alert is created for it.
notes.choices:
A) An alert is created at once
B) An alert is created with no fix version
C) No Dependabot alert is created for it
D) An alert is created after 72 hours
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: only GitHub-reviewed advisories raise alerts. B is wrong: no alert is raised at all, with or without a fix version. D is wrong: 72 hours relates to publishing repository advisories and CVE requests.
notes.explanation: Dependabot does not alert on unreviewed advisories, which are not checked for validity or completion.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advisory database”, “Unreviewed vulnerability advisories”
notes.evidence: Dependabot doesn't create Dependabot alerts for unreviewed advisories

notes.front: A malware advisory names a package your team installed last month. Which action matches the Docs?
notes.back: C: Remove the package and find an alternative, more secure replacement.
notes.choices:
A) Update to the fix version in the advisory
B) Wait for GitHub to review the advisory
C) Remove the package and find an alternative, more secure replacement
D) Dismiss it, since malware is usually accidental
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: malware alerts do not contain a fix version. B is wrong: malware advisories are published automatically. D is wrong: malware is intentional; it is vulnerabilities that are usually accidental.
notes.explanation: Malware has no safe versions, so there is no version to update to.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advisory database”, “Types of security advisories”
notes.evidence: You need to remove the malware from your project and find an alternative, more secure replacement for the dependency.

notes.front: Two alerts: one Critical with an EPSS score of 0.01, one High with 0.65. Which is more likely to be exploited in the next 30 days?
notes.back: C: The High one, because EPSS measures the probability of exploitation.
notes.choices:
A) Neither: EPSS applies only to malware
B) The Critical one, because CVSS measures the probability of exploitation
C) The High one, because EPSS measures the probability of exploitation
D) They are equally likely
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: CVSS gives the severity level, not likelihood. A is wrong: EPSS scores cover advisories containing CVEs with EPSS data. D is wrong: their EPSS scores differ.
notes.explanation: CVSS level describes severity; EPSS describes likelihood of exploitation.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advisory database”, “EPSS scores”
notes.evidence: the higher the score, the greater the probability that a vulnerability will be exploited.

notes.front: A dashboard shows an advisory’s EPSS as 3% at the 92nd percentile. A colleague says “92% chance it gets exploited”. What is right?
notes.back: B: 3% is the chance of exploitation in 30 days; the 92nd percentile means it outranks 92% of scored vulnerabilities.
notes.choices:
A) The colleague is right
B) 3% is the chance of exploitation in 30 days; the 92nd percentile means it outranks 92% of scored vulnerabilities
C) 92% is the CVSS severity
D) The percentile is the chance over one year
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: the percentile is a rank, not a probability. C is wrong: CVSS uses levels such as High, not this percentile. D is wrong: the Docs describe no one-year figure.
notes.explanation: The score is a probability; the percentile is a relative rank.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advisory database”, “EPSS scores”
notes.evidence: which is the proportion of all scored vulnerabilities with the same or a lower EPSS score.

notes.front: Olu maintains a public npm package, has fixed a flaw in a draft repository security advisory, and has no CVE number. What can he do?
notes.back: D: Request a CVE identification number from GitHub, which is a CNA.
notes.choices:
A) Wait until the advisory is public, because requests make it public
B) Publish without one; CVEs are only for unreviewed advisories
C) Use the GHSA ID as his CVE number
D) Request a CVE identification number from GitHub, which is a CNA
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: requesting a number does not make the advisory public. C is wrong: a GHSA ID is GitHub’s own identifier, not a CVE. B is wrong: nothing limits CVEs to unreviewed advisories.
notes.explanation: GitHub can assign CVE numbers, and usually reviews requests within 72 hours.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Repository security advisories”, “CVE identification numbers”
notes.evidence: you can request a CVE identification number from GitHub. GitHub usually reviews the request within 72 hours.

notes.front: A project’s vendor is its own CNA and has already assigned a CVE. The maintainers draft a GitHub advisory. What should they do about the CVE?
notes.back: C: Add the existing CVE to the security advisory form.
notes.choices:
A) Leave the CVE out, since GitHub will import it
B) Request a second CVE from GitHub
C) Add the existing CVE to the security advisory form
D) Replace it with a GHSA ID
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: GitHub cannot assign CVEs to a project covered by another CNA. A is wrong: the Docs say to add it to the form. D is wrong: every advisory already gets a GHSA ID; it does not replace a CVE.
notes.explanation: GitHub cannot assign CVEs to a project covered by another CNA.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Repository security advisories”, “CVE identification numbers”
notes.evidence: If you already have a CVE you want to use, for example, if you use a CVE Numbering Authority (CNA) other than GitHub, add the CVE to the security advisory form.

notes.front: A researcher privately reports a flaw in a public repository. The maintainers want to work on a fix out of public view, then announce it. Which feature fits?
notes.back: B: A repository security advisory, with a temporary private fork for the fix.
notes.choices:
A) Open a public issue labelled “security”
B) A repository security advisory, with a temporary private fork for the fix
C) Submit a community contribution to the GitHub Advisory Database
D) Wait for the National Vulnerability Database to publish it
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: an issue is public. C is wrong: community contributions improve published global advisories. D is wrong: that gives the maintainers no private workspace.
notes.explanation: Repository security advisories exist to discuss and fix vulnerabilities privately before publishing.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Repository security advisories”, “About repository security advisories”
notes.evidence: Privately collaborate to fix the vulnerability in a temporary private fork.

notes.front: A maintainer must publish an advisory now, but the fix is still in development. What do the Docs advise?
notes.back: D: Mention in the advisory that a fix is in development, then edit it after publication.
notes.choices:
A) Invent a future version number as the fix version
B) Never publish until a fix exists
C) Mark the advisory as malware
D) Mention in the advisory that a fix is in development, then edit it after publication
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: nothing in the Docs supports an invented version. B is wrong: that advice is for fixes that are imminently available. C is wrong: malware is for malicious packages.
notes.explanation: Without a fix version, users are alerted with no safe version to update to.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Repository security advisories”, “Importance of fix versions”
notes.evidence: In development but not yet available**, mention this in the advisory, and edit the advisory later, after publication.

notes.front: A script must check that strings are GHSA IDs. Which string is valid?
notes.back: C: `GHSA-7xg2-q9jm-c4vw`.
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: letters after the prefix must be lowercase. A is wrong: 1, a, b, d, e and i are not in the allowed set. D is wrong: that is a CVE identifier.
notes.explanation: All three groups are four lowercase characters from `23456789cfghjmpqrvwx`.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advisory database”, “GHSA IDs”
notes.evidence: All letters are lowercase.

notes.front: For which of these would GitHub review a vulnerability advisory: (1) a package from pypi.org; (2) an action from GitHub Marketplace; (3) a package only on a company’s private registry?
notes.back: (1) yes; (2) yes; (3) no: GitHub reviews advisories for packages from a supported registry.
notes.explanation: Pip and GitHub Actions are supported ecosystems; a private registry is not in the list.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advisory database”, “GitHub-reviewed vulnerability advisories”
notes.evidence: We review advisories if they are for a vulnerability in a package that comes from a supported registry.

notes.front: Kofi publishes a security advisory from his fork of a popular library. His fork owns no package on any public registry. Will GitHub send Dependabot alerts from it?
notes.back: B: No. From a fork, alerts are sent only if the fork owns a uniquely named package on a public registry.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, to every repository that uses the original library
B) No. From a fork, alerts are sent only if the fork owns a uniquely named package on a public registry
C) Yes, but only after a CVE is assigned
D) Only if the advisory is unreviewed
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: the fork rule limits alerts. C is wrong: the Docs tie fork alerts to package ownership, not to a CVE. D is wrong: unreviewed advisories never raise Dependabot alerts.
notes.explanation: GitHub reviews every published advisory but may or may not use it to send alerts.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Repository security advisories”, “Dependabot alerts for published security advisories”
notes.evidence: If the security advisory comes from a fork, we'll only send an alert if the fork owns a package, published under a unique name, on a public package registry.

notes.front: Which advisory type is each: (1) imported straight from the National Vulnerability Database feed; (2) from the OpenSSF Malicious Packages repository; (3) checked by GitHub and mapped to an npm package?
notes.back: (1) unreviewed; (2) malware; (3) GitHub-reviewed.
notes.explanation: The three types differ by source and by whether GitHub has reviewed them.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advisory database”, “Malware advisories”
notes.evidence: Malware** advisories are advisories about malicious open source packages. We publish them automatically into the GitHub Advisory Database from the npm security team and the [OpenSSF Malicious Packages](https://github.com/ossf/malicious-packages) repository.

notes.front: Which identifier is each: (1) `GHSA-4mcv-vh8q-8r2x`; (2) `CVE-2023-4863`; (3) `CWE-400`?
notes.back: (1) a GHSA ID for an advisory; (2) a CVE for one vulnerability; (3) a CWE for a weakness type.
notes.explanation: Every advisory has a GHSA ID; CVEs and CWEs come from outside GitHub.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advisory database”, “GHSA IDs”
notes.evidence: Each security advisory, regardless of its type, has a unique identifier referred to as a GHSA ID.

notes.front: Which CVSS versions can each advisory carry: (1) a CVE GitHub obtained for a maintainer; (2) an imported CVE?
notes.explanation: Only imported CVEs can carry version 3.0.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advisory database”, “CVSS levels”
notes.evidence: If the CVE is imported, the GitHub Advisory Database supports CVSS versions 4.0, 3.1 and 3.0.

notes.front: A tool reads advisories straight from GitHub’s published files. Which format and file type should it expect?
notes.back: The Open Source Vulnerability (OSV) format, as `JSON` files.
notes.explanation: That is how the GitHub Advisory Database publishes its advisories.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advisory database”, “About the GitHub Advisory Database”
notes.evidence: Security advisories are published as JSON files in the Open Source Vulnerability (OSV) format.
